analysis.one_liner: Requires standardized front-of-package nutrition labels with warnings for foods high in sugar, salt, or fat.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in August 2021 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to create a standardized label on the front of food packages that rates a product's overall nutritional value and flags items high in saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, or added sugars. It also would have tightened claims like "whole grain," "fruit," and "natural," required caffeine and phosphorus disclosures, strengthened allergen labeling, and made full label information available at online checkout. It died in committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary shoppers, especially people managing diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, food allergies, or celiac disease. A standardized front-of-package label with warning symbols would let them judge a product at a glance, without decoding fine-print ingredient lists, and would let people with allergies and gluten sensitivities see allergen information when buying food online. The bill would also have pushed manufacturers to disclose how little actual fruit or whole grain is in products marketed with those images and words.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers and people with food allergies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to set a standardized front-of-package symbol system that shows calories and flags saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, and added sugars, and that ranks foods by overall health value, such as a stop-light or star system.
Requires foods claiming "whole wheat," "whole grain," "fruit," or "vegetable" to disclose the actual percentage or serving amount of those ingredients, so shoppers can see how much is really inside.
Requires the FDA to define what "natural" means on food labels and to force disclosure of added artificial dyes, flavorings, sweeteners, sugar alcohols, and isolated fibers.
Requires all label information to be available to shoppers at the online point of sale, and requires the FDA to publish a searchable public database of every packaged food's label information.
Strengthens allergen labeling, lets the FDA designate additional major food allergens, and requires allergen information for unpackaged foods sold at retail and for online purchases.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food manufacturers, who would have had to redesign labels, verify grain and fruit content, reformulate or rebrand products that earn warning symbols, and submit label information to a public FDA database. Some of those costs would likely be passed to shoppers as higher prices, and products high in sugar or salt could see lower sales as their labels discourage purchases.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes sweeping new rulemaking on the FDA with firm deadlines — proposed rules within one year and final rules within two — and makes proposed rules final automatically if the agency misses its deadline, which is an aggressive approach that overrides the usual notice-and-comment process for parts of the rules.

The new definition of "artificial" sweeps in ingredients like corn syrup, maltodextrin, and cocoa processed with alkali, and the bill would have constrained marketing terms like "whole grain" and "fruit" that many food companies have built brands around, so compliance and litigation costs would be substantial and could fall partly on consumers as higher prices.

The bill gives small online sellers an exemption (under $500,000 in annual sales) but otherwise applies to all packaged foods, and mandatory warning-style labels can push companies toward reformulating products in ways that do not always make them genuinely healthier.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well supported: clearer front-of-package information helps people make faster, better-informed choices about sugar, salt, fat, and allergens, and the online-labeling provision fills a genuine gap as more food is bought online. The costs fall on manufacturers and add rulemaking burdens, and a poorly designed rating system could mislead as much as inform — but the bill gave the FDA flexibility in choosing the system and required periodic evaluation of whether it actually works. On balance, the benefits to shoppers outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee from August 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, with no markup, no vote, and no action in the Senate.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on August 3, 2021, with Rep. Rosa DeLauro as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded.
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill would have required the FDA to establish a standardized front-of-package nutrition labeling system with warning symbols for foods high in saturated fat, trans fat, sodium, and added sugars.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided new front-of-package warning labels, stricter definitions of claims like "natural" and "healthy," and a public database of all their label information. Shoppers did not get the labels the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the bill was never brought to a vote, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would have forced standardized front-of-package ratings and warning symbols for foods high in saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars, plus disclosure of actual whole grain and fruit content and a public database of all label information. The industry's interest in avoiding these disclosures runs against shoppers' interest in seeing them, since a warning label can directly cut sales of the products most in need of disclosure.

industries.industry: Online grocers and e-commerce food retailers
industries.note: Sellers would have had to display full label information at the online point of selection, a real compliance cost, but shoppers buying food online currently cannot see labels at checkout; small retailers under $500,000 in annual sales were exempt.
